findings.text: The first paragraph tells a newcomer what Athena is and what sets it apart, in plain words. A newcomer could repeat it.
findings.source: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository. It shows how it read the request, has one AI model do the work and a different one check it, and records what each step cost."

findings.text: The header says why this page exists: it is a demonstration. The Claims and sources section backs this up, with file and line links for every claim at a fixed commit.
findings.source: "Athena made this study of firstmate to show that it can read an unfamiliar project and explain it with every statement traced to a claim, and every claim to lines in the project's own files."

findings.text: Almost all of the page is about firstmate, a different project, so a newcomer who came to learn about Athena gets one paragraph on Athena and dozens of cards on another tool. They have to work out for themselves that the firstmate content is only a sample.
findings.source: Heading "Athena explains how firstmate handles work" and the sections States, Counters, Transitions, Why it is built this way

findings.text: The transition and design cards are packed with firstmate details (exit codes, locks, places-held, close-pending). This suits someone studying firstmate, not someone deciding whether Athena is useful.
findings.source: Transitions card t2: "Every worker place is held, so the spawn is deferred with exit 75 and the item stays queued. A spawn that cannot take the project lock, or cannot read the capacity declaration, exits 1 instead and does not wait."

findings.text: Terms are defined before they are used, and the page says plainly where its sources are silent, so readers who do go through the firstmate content can follow it.
findings.source: Heading "Words used first" and the note on in scope: "The cited instruction does not say what makes work in scope, so this page gives no test for it."

findings.text: The next steps are easy to find (there is also a link in the header), but they leave out the clone command, any prerequisites such as a Rust toolchain or model access, and where to run `athena ask`.
findings.source: Next steps: "Install Athena from a checkout of its repository: ./setup.sh" and "Try it with a one-line request: athena ask "add a changelog""

findings.text: Being open about limits builds trust with careful readers. But a newcomer meeting Athena for the first time learns that its showcase study missed whole areas on the first pass and that nothing was run.
findings.source: Limits of this study, f3: "A first reading of the pinned tree missed these paths... none was run, so no run confirmed that a script behaves as its header says."

findings.text: The page ends on internal details about where its data lives, which means nothing to a newcomer.
findings.source: About this page: "This page's study id, firstmate-work-handling, is the name of the folder under studies/ that holds the data this page is generated from."
